In the Go repo at /mnt/d/skywalking-banyandb/graphloom/879ee04f-e57 (apache/skywalking-banyandb), I'm researching a performance design (tag aggregation over the measure query engine; see docs/design/0.12.0/tag-aggregation/README.md §7.2 "Time-bucket grouping" and §7.7 "The local scan"). The design was mostly implemented by PR #1360. I need the CURRENT state of the vectorized aggregation operator code.

Please find and report (with file paths, line numbers, and relevant code snippets):

1. `BatchAggregation` struct and its `Consume` method (design doc cites `pkg/query/vectorized/measure/aggregation.go` — exact package path may differ, search for it). Show how `Consume` iterates rows: does it call `computeKey` per row, probe `a.groups[key]`, and fold? Show `computeKey` (design doc cites aggregation.go:523) and confirm whether it allocates a string per row (`string(buf)`).

2. `appendKeyComponent` in `groupby.go` (design doc cites groupby.go:287) — show its body, and confirm which column types it supports (int64, float64, string, bytes, *modelv1.TagValue, *modelv1.FieldValue) and what it does for array types (the design doc says it "silently returns the buffer unchanged" for arrays — confirm if that's still the current behavior or if it's been fixed).

3. The bucket streaming operator `BatchTimeBucket` (design doc §7.2) — find it (likely in the vectorized/measure package), show how it detects a "bucket advance" while scanning a time-ascending column — i.e., where does it compare the current row's bucket to the previous one? This is the same boundary-detection logic the issue's Phase A ("run-folding") wants to reuse for detecting `(series, bucket)` span boundaries.

4. `collectTagIndices` (design doc cites aggregation.go:252) — show its body, confirm whether it currently takes an exclusion index parameter (for HideTag) as the design doc describes, i.e. is this already implemented.

5. The `Distinct` interface / `distinct.go` in `pkg/query/aggregation` (design §7.3) — show it, and the `AggCountDistinct` function, and the `aggSlot` variant holding a set.

6. `fold` function (design doc cites aggregation.go:464) — show it, confirm COUNT does a null-check-only branch for non-numeric columns (not reading/parsing the value).

7. `model.MeasureAgg` struct (pkg/query/model/model.go or similar) — show its fields, confirm `TagName`, `TagFamily`, `HideTag`, and whether there's already any field marking a column as "index-resolved" (for plan-time) that stage 8a (run-folding) would need to add.

Report file:line references and relevant snippets directly. Keep report under 700 words of prose plus code snippets.

tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

entries.name: LSP
entries.description:
Interact with Language Server Protocol (LSP) servers to get code intelligence features.

Supported operations:
- goToDefinition: Find where a symbol is defined
- findReferences: Find all references to a symbol
- hover: Get hover information (documentation, type info) for a symbol
- documentSymbol: Get all symbols (functions, classes, variables) in a document
- workspaceSymbol: Search for symbols matching a query across the entire workspace
- goToImplementation: Find implementations of an interface or abstract method
- prepareCallHierarchy: Get call hierarchy item at a position (functions/methods)
- incomingCalls: Find all functions/methods that call the function at a position
- outgoingCalls: Find all functions/methods called by the function at a position

All operations require:
- filePath: The file to operate on
- line: The line number (1-based, as shown in editors)
- character: The character offset (1-based, as shown in editors)

The workspaceSymbol operation also takes:
- query: The symbol name or partial name to search for. Always provide it — most language servers return no results for an empty query.

Note: LSP servers must be configured for the file type. If no server is available, an error will be returned.

filePath.description: The absolute or relative path to the file

line.description: The line number (1-based, as shown in editors)

character.description: The character offset (1-based, as shown in editors)

query.description: The symbol name or partial name to search for (workspaceSymbol only). Most language servers return no results for an empty query, so always provide it when using workspaceSymbol.

entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

entries.name: SendMessage
entries.description:
# SendMessage

Send a message to another agent.

```json
{"to": "researcher", "summary": "assign task 1", "message": "start on task #1"}
```

| `to` | |
|---|---|
| `"researcher"` | Teammate by name |
| `"main"` | The main conversation (background subagents only) |
| `"worker"` | Any agent from `ListAgents` — subagent, another local Claude session |
| `"worker [3fa9c1]"` | Same, plus its `[ref]` — only when a listing or an error shows one |

Your plain text output is NOT visible to other agents — to communicate, you MUST call this tool. Messages from teammates are delivered automatically; you don't check an inbox. Refer to agents by name — names keep working after an agent completes (a send resumes it from its transcript). Use the raw `agentId` (format `a...-...`) from its spawn result only when the agent has no name, or when a newer agent took the name (latest wins). When relaying, don't quote the original — it's already rendered to the user.

## Cross-session

Use `ListAgents` to discover targets. Every row leads with the agent's `name [ref]` — the name IS the address; there is no separate address syntax.

```json
{"to": "worker", "message": "check if tests pass over there"}
{"to": "worker [3fa9c1]", "message": "you, specifically"}
```

Send the bare name — a name that exactly matches one live agent or session (on this machine, on another machine, or in the cloud) delivers directly. Append the ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — `ListAgents` shows two rows with it, or an error asks you to disambiguate (you typed only a prefix, or a session list could not be checked). A ref you did not just read from a listing or an error will not resolve, and if the same name also names an in-process agent, the bare name always wins — use the in-process one.

A listed peer is alive and will receive your message; messages enqueue and drain at the receiver's next tool round (its `ListAgents` row says whether it is busy or idle right now). A successful send means the message reached that session, not that its Claude read it: a session running in a different permission mode than yours holds cross-session messages for its user's approval (and may let them expire), and a session can refuse them outright — for a session on this machine a `[Cross-session delivery notice]` tells you when that happens (the tool result says when this session has no inbox for one to reach); for a Remote Control, cloud or Claude Desktop session nothing reports back, so never treat silence as agreement. Your message arrives wrapped as `<cross-session-message from="...">`. **To reply to an incoming message, copy its `from` attribute as your `to`.** Cross-session messages travel between SESSIONS: if you are a subagent, your send goes out under your parent session's address, and any reply is delivered to the parent session's conversation, not to you. The receiver reads your message literally in every case (idle or busy, on this machine, over Remote Control or headless): an `@` followed by a file path, or `@server:resource`, attaches nothing there, unlike in your own user's input. So never rely on `@` to deliver content: send the text itself, or a file with its own tool.

To hear when a session ON THIS MACHINE finishes what it is doing, pass `notify_when_idle: true` (from the main conversation only) — one-shot and opt-in: exactly one `[Cross-session idle notice]` arrives when it next goes idle (or exits) — shown to you, or only to your user when this session holds peer messages for approval (the tool result says which); if it never signals within the subscription's lifetime (it may still be busy, may refuse inbound requests, or may have ended abruptly) the notice says the subscription expired instead. Omit `message` for a pure subscription that costs that session nothing; include one to deliver it now AND subscribe. Never poll `ListAgents` in a loop or send "are you done?" messages instead.

Permission boundaries are per-session: NEVER ask a peer to perform an action that was denied or blocked in your session, or that you expect your own permission settings would block — a peer doing it for you bypasses the user's permission decision (cross-session permission laundering). Route blocked work back to your user instead.

## Protocol responses (legacy)

If you receive a JSON message with `type: "shutdown_request"` or `type: "plan_approval_request"`, respond with the matching `_response` type — echo the `request_id`, set `approve` true/false:

```json
{"to": "team-lead", "message": {"type": "shutdown_response", "request_id": "...", "approve": true}}
{"to": "researcher", "message": {"type": "plan_approval_response", "request_id": "...", "approve": false, "feedback": "add error handling"}}
```

Approving shutdown terminates your process. Rejecting plan sends the teammate back to revise. Don't originate `shutdown_request` unless asked. Don't send structured JSON status messages — report progress through your task tools if you have them, otherwise in plain prose.

to.description: Recipient: a name from ListAgents (append its " [ref]" only when a listing or an error shows one), a teammate name, "main", or a background agent's agentId

summary.description: A 5-10 word label for your own transcript row (not transmitted — the recipient previews the first line of `message`). Truncated to 200 characters rather than rejected.

anyOf.description: Plain text message content. The recipient's human sees only the FIRST LINE as a one-line preview until they expand it, so make the first line a clear, self-contained sentence saying what this is about — not a greeting, preamble, or bare @-mention.

notify_when_idle.description: Ask a session ON THIS MACHINE to send you ONE notice when it next goes idle (finishes its turn with nothing queued) or exits — opt-in, one-shot, no polling. With a message: deliver it now AND subscribe. Without a message (omit it): a pure subscription that costs the other session nothing.

content.content:
1	# Tag Aggregation and Time Bucketing in the Measure Query Engine
2	
3	Status: **design** — not implemented.
4	
5	This document specifies three additions to BanyanDB's existing measure query engine:
6	
7	1. aggregation over **tags**, not just fields;
8	2. an exact **`COUNT_DISTINCT`** function;
9	3. **time-bucket grouping** — `GROUP BY <bucket>, <tags>` producing a series, with the bucket
10	   width taken from the request or, failing that, from the measure's `interval`.
11	
12	They are separable features that share one API surface and one operator, and a dashboard needs
13	all three: (1) and (2) answer "how many distinct things", (3) answers "over time".
14	
15	(3) is driven by a separate requirement — converting analytical `GROUP BY <bucket>, <tags>` SQL
16	onto BanyanDB (§1.1) — not by the cardinality work. That conversion also needs two things this
17	document scopes out, multiple aggregates per request and result aliases; §3 records the gap.
18	
19	It is a companion to the [native inverted-index design](../native-inverted-index/README.md): the
20	scoping work for that package asked whether the native index should grow its own local
21	aggregation, and concluded it should not. Aggregation stays in the query engine, which already
22	reduces locally on data nodes and combines at the liaison; this design extends that machinery
23	rather than duplicating it.
24	
25	---
26	
27	## 1. Motivation
28	
29	Dashboards built on SkyWalking-shaped measures routinely need cardinality answers where the
30	interesting dimension is a **tag**, not a field. Take a per-api-key request-rate measure: the
31	user is the `service_id` tag, the api-key is the `entity_id` tag, and the only field is a scalar
32	request count. Three questions follow immediately.
33	
34	| Case | Question | SQL shape |
35	|---|---|---|
36	| **Scalar** | "how many distinct api-keys did one user use last week?" | `COUNT(DISTINCT entity_id) WHERE service_id = …` over a multi-bucket window |
37	| **Ranked** | "show every user, ranked by key count, page 3" | `GROUP BY service_id`, `ORDER BY COUNT(DISTINCT entity_id) DESC`, `LIMIT`/`OFFSET` |
38	| **Series** | "plot distinct api-keys per 5 minutes for the last hour" | `GROUP BY <time bucket>, service_id ORDER BY <time bucket> ASC` |
39	
40	The ranked case is what a dashboard row needs; the series case is what a dashboard *chart* needs.
41	Every realistic dashboard window spans many buckets, so the scalar case is never asked over a
42	single bucket either.
43	
44	The series case is the shape analytical SQL expresses with a bucketing function — PostgreSQL and
45	DataFusion spell it `DATE_BIN(INTERVAL <width>, time, <origin>)`, others `time_bucket` or
46	`GROUP BY FLOOR(time/width)`. The semantics this design adopts are that function's, with the
47	origin fixed at the Unix epoch: each row is assigned to `floor(timestamp / width) * width`, and
48	rows sharing a bucket and a tag key form one group.
49	
50	None of the three is expressible today.
51	
52	- `measurev1.QueryRequest.Aggregation` names only a **field**. `plan/analyzer.go:301
53	  validateAggField` walks `measureSchema.GetFields()` and rejects anything else.
54	- `modelv1.AggregationFunction` is `{MEAN, MAX, MIN, COUNT, SUM}` — there is no `COUNT_DISTINCT`.
55	- **There is no time bucketing anywhere in the measure query API.** `QueryRequest.GroupBy` is
56	  `{tag_projection, field_name}` — tags only; the timestamp is not addressable as a group key,
57	  and no interval/step/bin concept exists in `query.proto`. Worse, aggregation deliberately
58	  *discards* time: `buildAggOutputLayout` emits `[shard_id?] + tags + agg columns` with no
59	  `RoleTimestamp`, and `plan/build_test.go:221` pins it — *"aggregation output must drop
60	  timestamp (D2)"*. The row path agrees (`measure_plan_aggregation.go:286,342` build
61	  `DataPoint{TagFamilies: …}` and never set `Timestamp`). So `agg` collapses the entire
62	  `time_range` into one row per tag group, always.
63	
64	The workarounds all fail:
65	
66	1. **`COUNT(*)` over one bucket.** This leans on storage usually holding one row per
67	   `(entity, bucket)` — and `Measure.interval` is a **declared cadence, not an enforced
68	   invariant**. Writers may emit off-cadence: on a 1-minute measure, timestamps of `09:01:00`
69	   *and* `09:01:34` are both legal and both land in the 09:01 bucket. So the count can be wrong
70	   even inside a single bucket, and it is certainly wrong once the window spans two — measured at
71	   21 for 3 keys over 7 buckets. No error, just a plausible wrong number. This is the strongest
72	   argument for a real `COUNT_DISTINCT`: the shortcut it replaces has no invariant behind it,
73	   only a convention writers are free to break.
74	2. **`groupBy(entity_id)` and count rows client-side.** Correct at any window, but it ships one
75	   row per distinct value to the *client*, and it does not compose with `top` / `offset` /
76	   `limit`, so the ranked case cannot be rendered.
77	3. **One query per bucket.** Correct at any window — each individual query is the workaround-1
78	   shape, exact precisely because its window is one bucket wide — and it is the only workaround
79	   that still composes with ranking. The cost is a fan-out: a 1-hour window at 1-minute
80	   granularity is 60 round-trips, a day is 1440, and the caller carries the bucket arithmetic,
81	   the partial-failure handling and the reassembly.
82	
83	### 1.1 The driving requirement for time bucketing
84	
85	The series case is not a speculative extension of the cardinality work. It comes from a separate
86	requirement: converting existing analytical queries onto BanyanDB, where the canonical shape is
87	
88	> group by **a time bucket plus two or more tag dimensions**, select a `COUNT(DISTINCT <tag>)`
89	> over a further tag that is **not** carried as an output column, alias the result, and select
90	> additional aggregates alongside it in the same row.
91	
92	Read as a checklist, that shape is the fastest way to see what the design must cover:
93	
94	| Element of the shape | Requirement | Where |
95	|---|---|---|
96	| group by a time bucket | time-bucket group key, emitted as the row timestamp | §5.1, §7.2 |
97	| group by several tags as well | **multiple** tag group keys alongside the bucket | §5.1 |
98	| `COUNT(DISTINCT <tag>)` | `COUNT_DISTINCT` over a tag | §5.1, §7.4 |
99	| the distinct target is not an output column | target stripped from the output, not emitted as a first-seen tag | §5.2 |
100	| the result is aliased | a result alias | **out of scope** — §3 |
101	| further aggregates in the same row | more than one aggregate per request | **out of scope** — §3 |
102	
103	The last two rows are deliberately out of scope (§3). This design delivers the `COUNT_DISTINCT`
104	half of the shape; a caller converting such a query issues the distinct count as its own request
105	and names the result column client-side. That is a smaller step than the full conversion, and
106	saying so plainly is better than implying the checklist is fully served.
107	
108	Two further notes on mapping this query onto a measure:
109	
110	- **All group tags must live in one tag family.** `distributedGroupByTagNames`
111	  (`distributed.go:1131`) reads `families[0]` only, so the tag dimensions grouped alongside the
112	  bucket must share a family. This is a pre-existing v1 limitation, not one this design adds, but
113	  it constrains the schema the conversion targets.
114	- **The effective routing key determines whether the distinct pushes down** (§7.4) — the
115	  measure's `sharding_key` when set, otherwise its entity. The condition is
116	  `routingTags ⊆ groupByTags ∪ {target}`, so a routing key drawn from the grouped tags plus the
117	  distinct target pushes down; a routing tag outside that set gets the query rejected. A
118	  conversion gets to *choose* its routing key, so this is a modelling instruction rather than a
119	  constraint discovered too late.
120	- **The query must resolve to a single stage** (§7.4). Multi-stage `COUNT_DISTINCT` is rejected,
121	  and an empty `stages` falls back to `DefaultStages` — so this is a constraint on the target
122	  group's lifecycle configuration, not just on the query text.
123	
124	The gap is narrow and the engine already has every primitive needed to close it: grouping over
125	tag columns, a Map/Reduce split across data nodes and the liaison, a per-query memory budget,
126	top-N/pagination over an aggregate output column, and — for the series case — an
127	epoch-anchored bucketing formula already in the tree (`getWindowStart` in
128	`pkg/flow/streaming/sliding_window.go:302`, used by the TopN pre-aggregation path).
129	
130	**Time bucketing and tag aggregation are orthogonal**, and the series case needs both. They would
131	be near-interchangeable if a measure held exactly one row per `(entity, interval)` — then
132	counting rows in a bucket would count distinct entities. It does not: the interval is a declared
133	cadence, so two rows for one entity can share a bucket. `COUNT` grouped by bucket therefore
134	answers "how many data points", `COUNT_DISTINCT` answers "how many distinct things", and they
135	diverge whenever a writer emits off-cadence or a query bucket is coarser than the interval.
136	Shipping either feature alone leaves half the dashboard unservable.
137

140	## 2. Requirements
141	
142	- `agg` may target a **tag** as well as a field.
143	- A new `COUNT_DISTINCT` function, **exact** (not sketch-based).
144	- `group_by` may key on a **time bucket**, producing one row per `(bucket, tag group)` and a
145	  timestamp on each result row. The width comes from the request or from the measure's
146	  `interval` — see §5.3.
147	- Bucket grouping must **stream node-locally**: on the part path, live state is one bucket rather
148	  than the whole window, and a node emits a bucket as it closes instead of withholding until its
149	  scan ends (§7.2). This is a requirement rather than an optimisation — it is what makes a
150	  day-long query at 1-minute buckets viable at all. It is explicitly **not** an end-to-end
151	  pipelining promise: the liaison collects node frames before reducing them, so the *query*
152	  remains request/response even where the *operator* streams. Index mode does not stream at all
153	  (§7.2).
154	- All of the above compose with each other and with the existing `top`, `offset` and `limit`, in
155	  standalone **and** distributed deployments.
156	- A high-cardinality target must fail loudly against the per-query budget, never OOM a node.
157	- `COUNT_DISTINCT` **pushes down to the data nodes like every other function**, with a scalar
158	  partial. A request that cannot be pushed down is **rejected at analyze time** — there is no
159	  second, costlier execution path (§7.4).
160	- **`index_mode` measures are in scope** for both grouping and aggregation, on the same terms as
161	  part-backed measures (§7.4, §7.7).
162	- Reachable from BydbQL, not only from clients that hand-build a `QueryRequest`.
163	- Default behaviour is unchanged: a request with no `time_bucket` still collapses the whole
164	  `time_range`, exactly as today.
165	
166	## 3. Non-goals
167	
168	- **Approximate distinct (HyperLogLog).** Constant wire cost is attractive, but it needs a new
169	  partial wire type and an API contract about error bounds. The cardinality of the motivating
170	  case (api-keys per user) does not justify either. Revisit only if a deployment actually hits
171	  the budget.
172	
173	> **Decided:** the two entries below are out of scope. `COUNT_DISTINCT` is the piece of §1.1 this
174	> design delivers; the remaining elements of that query shape are deferred deliberately, not left
175	> open. A caller converting such a query issues the distinct count as its own request and names
176	> the result column client-side.
177	
178	- **Multiple aggregates in one request.** `QueryRequest.agg` stays singular and BydbQL keeps
179	  erroring on a second aggregate in `SELECT`. The operator is already plural — `AggSpec` is a
180	  slice and `BatchAggregation` loops over `a.aggs` — so if this is ever picked up the work is API
181	  and planning rather than execution, and it can be added as `repeated Aggregation` under a new
182	  field number without breaking the singular form.
183	- **Result aliases (`AS`).** No BydbQL `AS` production and no `Aggregation.output_name`. The
184	  result column keeps the naming rule in §5.2: it is named after the aggregation target.
185	- **Row-path parity.** See §8.
186	- **`COUNT_DISTINCT` in `TopNAggregation` pre-aggregation rules.** Rejected, not implemented.
187	- **Per-bucket `top`.** With `time_bucket` set, `top`/`offset`/`limit` stay **global** over the
188	  whole result set — one heap, exactly today's semantics. "Top 10 devices *in each* bucket" is
189	  the TopN RPC's job and already exists there: `TopNResponse.lists` is "a series topN lists
190	  ranked by timestamp". Redefining `top` per bucket would fork that semantics across two APIs.
191	  See §10 for the consequence this has for `limit`.
192	- **Bucket gap-filling.** Buckets with no data produce no row. Zero-filling a sparse series is a
193	  presentation concern and needs the client to know the expected bucket set anyway.
194	- **Arbitrary bucket origins.** Buckets are anchored at the Unix epoch, matching the `DATE_BIN`
195	  call above with `TIMESTAMP '1970-01-01 00:00:00'`. A configurable origin is not in scope.
196	
197	**Current limitation, not a design decision: `group_by.time_bucket` requires `agg`.** This
198	document never states whether a *raw* bucketed `GroupBy` (`time_bucket` set, no `agg`) is
199	supported — it is written throughout as if `agg` is always present. Implementing §7.2 found a
200	concrete reason it cannot be, as things stand: the no-`agg` shape reuses `BatchAggregation`'s
201	empty-`AggSpec` output layout, which — unlike `BatchGroupByFirst`, the row-preserving raw-GroupBy
202	operator — does not carry the full input schema forward (it drops other fields, the series id,
203	and the version), and the distributed row-merge path has no bucket-aware counterpart either. The
204	analyzer rejects this combination explicitly (`plan.Analyze: time_bucket requires Agg`) rather
205	than shipping a silently-truncated result. Lifting this is legitimate future work, but it needs
206	schema-preservation and distributed-merge work of its own; it is not a small extension of the
207	`agg` case.

211	## 4. Background: how measure aggregation works today
212	
213	The vectorized engine is the default (`vectorized/measure/config.go DefaultConfig` → `Enabled:
214	true`); the row engine in `pkg/query/logical/measure` is explicitly marked *"Do not extend with
215	new features"* (`measure_analyzer.go:62-68`).
216	
217	**Standalone.** `plan.Analyze` builds a `GroupByAgg` node which `BuildOperators`
218	(`vectorized/measure/plan.go:61`) turns into one `BatchAggregation`. Group keys are encoded by
219	`appendKeyComponent` (`groupby.go:287`) — a shared helper that handles int64, float64, string,
220	bytes, `*modelv1.TagValue` and `*modelv1.FieldValue`. Each group holds one `aggSlot` per
221	aggregate, backed by `pkg/query/aggregation`.
222	
223	**Distributed.** The liaison sets `InternalQueryRequest.AggReturnPartial`
224	(`plan/distributed.go:474`), which the data node turns into `AggModeMap`
225	(`plan/dispatch.go:120-123`). The node emits typed-column *partials* — a `Partial{Value, Count}`
226	per group — serialized by `vectorized/measure/frame`. The liaison runs `AggModeReduce`
227	(`reduce.go:107 ReducePartialBatches`), deduplicating replicas on `(shard_id, group_key)` before
228	combining.
229	
230	Two structural facts this design leans on:
231	
232	- **Tag columns cross the wire fine.** The frame codec carries string and bytes columns with
233	  their family name intact (`frame/encode.go:65-69`, `decode.go:105-107`). The raw-GroupBy
234	  distributed path (`distributed.go:913 applyBatchGroupByFirstToRows`) already ships tag columns
235	  from data nodes and dedupes them liaison-side. Only array columns have no wire type
236	  (`frame/frame.go:185-202` → `ErrUnsupportedColumnType`).
237	- **A tag is only a *native typed* column when something keys off it.** `BuildBatchSchema`
238	  (`integration.go:60`) consults `buildNativeTagSet` (`:139`), which today contains only GroupBy
239	  keys. Every other tag stays a `ColumnTypeTagValue` passthrough. This matters because
240	  `aggregation.go:464 fold` hard-casts to `TypedColumn[int64]`/`[float64]` with no fallback.

244	## 5. API
245	
246	### 5.1 Proto
247	
248	One enum value in `api/proto/banyandb/model/v1/common.proto`:
249	
250	```proto
251	enum AggregationFunction {
252	  …
253	  AGGREGATION_FUNCTION_SUM = 5;
254	  // COUNT_DISTINCT counts the distinct non-null values of the target.
255	  // It is exact and bounded by the per-query memory budget.
256	  AGGREGATION_FUNCTION_COUNT_DISTINCT = 6;
257	}
258	```
259	
260	One field on `QueryRequest.Aggregation` in `api/proto/banyandb/measure/v1/query.proto`:
261	
262	```proto
263	message Aggregation {
264	  model.v1.AggregationFunction function = 1;
265	  // field_name must be one of files indicated by the field_projection
266	  string field_name = 2;
267	  // tag_name aggregates over a tag instead of a field. Exactly one of
268	  // field_name and tag_name must be set.
269	  string tag_name = 3;
270	}
271	```
272	
273	One field on `QueryRequest.GroupBy`, in the same file:
274	
275	```proto
276	message GroupBy {
277	  // tag_projection must be a subset of the tag_projection of QueryRequest
278	  model.v1.TagProjection tag_projection = 1;
279	  // field_name must be one of fields indicated by field_projection
280	  string field_name = 2;
281	  message TimeBucket {
282	    // width is a duration string using the same units as Measure.interval
283	    // ("ns", "us", "ms", "s", "m", "h", "d"). Empty means "use the measure's
284	    // interval"; if the measure has no interval either, the request is
285	    // rejected.
286	    string width = 1;
287	  }
288	  // time_bucket adds the data point's timestamp, floored to a bucket boundary,
289	  // as the leading group key, and re-emits it as the result row's timestamp.
290	  // Buckets are anchored at the Unix epoch: bucket_start = ts - ts % width,
291	  // matching DATE_BIN with a Unix-epoch origin. Unset means no time bucketing
292	  // — the whole time_range collapses to one row per tag group, as today.
293	  TimeBucket time_bucket = 3;
294	}
295	```
296	
297	All additions are wire-compatible; existing clients are unaffected, and an unset `time_bucket`
298	preserves today's behaviour exactly.
299	
300	**The aggregation target is qualified by family.** An earlier draft used a bare `tag_name`,
301	reasoning that the engine keys tag specs by bare name
302	(`pkg/query/logical/schema.go:92-99`) and so names must be unique. That is an implementation
303	assumption, not a schema invariant — and the two are not the same thing. Tag-family validation
304	(`api/validate/validate.go:329-347`) does not reject a name repeated across families;
305	`pkg/pb/v1/metadata.go:27-35` makes the same unenforced assumption; and
306	`pkg/query/vectorized/schema_test.go:81-94` explicitly exercises identical names in different
307	families. `RegisterTag` silently overwrites one family's spec with another's.
308	
309	So a bare name can be ambiguous on a valid schema. Two ways out were available: retrofit a global
310	uniqueness rule, or qualify at the new seam. **Qualifying is the correct one** — a uniqueness
311	rule would invalidate existing schemas that are legal today, to serve a feature they do not use.
312	`GroupBy` already qualifies by family; the aggregation target now matches it.
313	
314	### 5.2 Result naming
315	
316	The result column **inherits the target's name**, extending the existing field rule
317	(`plan.go:109-116`, pinned by `plan_test.go
318	TestBuildOperators_AggOutputName_InheritsInputFieldName`). So
319	`COUNT_DISTINCT(entity_id) GROUP BY service_id` returns tag `service_id` plus field `entity_id`,
320	and the ranked case orders with `top.field_name = "entity_id"` — no new API surface for ordering.
321	
322	When the analyzer injects the target tag into the tag projection itself (the caller did not ask
323	for it), that tag is **stripped from the output**. Otherwise every result row would also carry a
324	meaningless first-seen copy of the value being counted. If the caller *does* project the tag
325	explicitly, they get both a tag and a field of that name; the two live in separate namespaces
326	(`BatchSchema.tagByPath`, keyed by `(family, name)`, vs `fieldByName`) so nothing collides.
327	
328	The bucket has no such naming question: it is carried on `DataPoint.timestamp`, a field the
329	message already has, set to the **bucket start**. There is no synthetic `time_bucket` tag or
330	field — the wire shape of a bucketed result is the wire shape of any other data point.
331	
332	### 5.3 Resolving the bucket width
333	
334	The width comes from the request, or failing that from the measure. Either source is enough;
335	only the absence of both is an error.
336	
337	| `time_bucket` | `Measure.interval` | Outcome |
338	|---|---|---|
339	| unset | — | No bucketing. Today's behaviour, unchanged. |
340	| set, `width` given | — | Bucket width = `width`. |
341	| set, `width` empty | set | Bucket width = the measure's interval. |
342	| set, `width` empty | empty | **Reject** — *"time_bucket needs a width: measure %q declares no interval"*. |
343	| set, `width` unparseable / zero / negative | — | Reject. |
344	
345	Both sources are parsed with `timestamp.ParseDuration` (`pkg/timestamp/duration.go:31`), the same
346	parser the write path uses on the schema field (`banyand/measure/measure.go:118`), so the two
347	agree on units by construction.
348	
349	**There is deliberately no "must be a multiple of the interval" rule.** An earlier draft required
350	one, on the reasoning that a narrower or non-aligned bucket would partition the data
351	arbitrarily. That reasoning assumed `Measure.interval` describes where data points actually land
352	— and it does not. The field declares a *cadence writers are asked to follow*, not an invariant
353	storage enforces: on a 1-minute measure, timestamps of `09:01:00` and `09:01:34` are both legal.
354	
355	Once points may fall anywhere, every width is equally meaningful — binning arbitrary timestamps
356	is exactly what `DATE_BIN` does — and a multiple-of rule would reject useful queries to protect
357	an alignment that was never guaranteed. What survives from that reasoning is a cost observation
358	rather than a constraint: bucket count is `time_range / width`, so a very small width against a
359	long window produces many groups. That is bounded by the memory budget (§7.6) and by `limit`
360	(§10), which is where cost belongs.
361	
362	The same correction removes an assumption that ran deeper than this section — see §1 on why
363	`COUNT(*)` is unreliable even within a single bucket, and §11 on the test that assumption would
364	have produced.
365	
366	### 5.4 BydbQL
367	
368	```sql
369	SELECT service_id, COUNT(DISTINCT entity_id) FROM MEASURE … GROUP BY service_id
370	SELECT host, COUNT(host) FROM MEASURE … GROUP BY TIME_BUCKET('5m'), host
371	```
372	
373	`DISTINCT` is accepted inside `COUNT` only; `SUM(DISTINCT …)` is a parse error. The aggregate
374	column resolves against tags as well as fields — `transformer.go:846 convertAggregation`
375	currently hard-errors when the column is not in `allFields`.
376	
377	`TIME_BUCKET(<duration>)` is a pseudo-column accepted only in `GROUP BY`, at most once, and it
378	maps to `GroupBy.time_bucket`. The argument may be omitted — `TIME_BUCKET()` requests bucketing
379	at the measure's own interval, the `width`-empty case in §5.3. It is deliberately not selectable
380	in the projection: the bucket arrives on the data point's timestamp, not as a column. Results are
381	ordered by bucket ascending (§7.5), so an explicit `ORDER BY` on the bucket is unnecessary.

385	## 6. Semantics
386	
387	Validated at analyze time; anything outside the matrix is a hard error naming the target and its
388	type.
389	
390	| Target type | SUM / MIN / MAX / MEAN | COUNT | COUNT_DISTINCT |
391	|---|---|---|---|
392	| Field INT / FLOAT | ✅ today | ✅ today | ✅ new |
393	| Tag `TAG_TYPE_INT` | ✅ new | ✅ new | ✅ new |
394	| Tag `TAG_TYPE_STRING` | ❌ reject | ✅ new | ✅ new |
395	| Tag `TAG_TYPE_DATA_BINARY` | ❌ reject | ✅ new | ✅ new |
396	| Tag `*_ARRAY`, `TAG_TYPE_TIMESTAMP` | ❌ reject | ❌ reject | ❌ reject |
397	
398	- Null values are excluded, matching the current field behaviour: they do not increment `COUNT`
399	  and do not enter the distinct set.
400	- `MEAN` over an INT tag yields float64, matching the existing field rule.
401	- **Array and timestamp tags must be rejected explicitly, not left to fall through.**
402	  `tagTypeToColumnType` (`integration.go:162`) already errors on `TIMESTAMP`, but array tags map
403	  to `ColumnTypeInt64Array`/`ColumnTypeStrArray`, and `appendKeyComponent`
404	  (`groupby.go:287-303`) *silently returns the buffer unchanged* for those — every row would
405	  collapse into one group and produce a plausible wrong count, the exact failure mode this
406	  design exists to remove. A `keyComponentSupported(ColumnType) bool` predicate should sit next
407	  to `appendKeyComponent` so the analyzer's rejection list and the operator's assumption cannot
408	  drift apart.
409	
410	Time bucketing is orthogonal to this matrix: it adds a group key, not an aggregate, so it
411	composes with every cell above. Its own validation rules are in §5.3. Two interactions are worth
412	stating explicitly:
413	
414	- **A bucket key does not change what an aggregate means** — it only narrows the row set each
415	  aggregate sees. `COUNT_DISTINCT` per bucket counts values distinct *within* that bucket; a
416	  value present in two buckets counts once in each. That is the intended series semantics, and it
417	  is deliberately not the same number as the unbucketed total.
418	- **`TAG_TYPE_TIMESTAMP` tags remain rejected** as aggregation targets. The bucket key comes from
419	  the data point's own timestamp, which is not a tag, so the two never meet.

424	
425	### 7.1 Binding the target to a column
426	
427	`model.MeasureAgg` gains `TagName`, `TagFamily` and `HideTag` (the last set when the analyzer
428	injected the projection). Four existing seams become target-aware:
429	
430	| Seam | Change |
431	|---|---|
432	| `plan/analyzer.go:209 translateAgg` | resolve tag **or** field; enforce the §6 matrix |
433	| `plan/analyzer.go:264 ensureAggFieldProjected` | mirror `ensureGroupByProjected` (`:226`) and inject the tag, setting `HideTag` |

440	
441	Everything downstream of `AggSpec.InputCol` is index-based, so **SUM/MIN/MAX/MEAN/COUNT over an
442	INT tag need no execution changes at all** — the partial is a `RoleField` int64/float64 column
443	named after the target, exactly what `bindAggReduceSpecs` (`reduce.go:219`) already binds. Only
444	two small operator fixes are needed:
445	
446	- `aggregation.go:464 fold` — `COUNT` must not read the value for non-numeric columns (it
447	  currently parses, then calls `In(v)`). A null-check-only branch makes `COUNT(string_tag)` work.
448	- `aggregation.go:252 collectTagIndices` — accept an exclusion index so a `HideTag` target is

450	
451	### 7.2 Time-bucket grouping
452	
453	The implementation is one small map operator plus one conditional in the output layout. The key
454	insight is that **the timestamp is already an `int64` column** in the input schema
455	(`RoleTimestamp`, produced by `BuildBatchSchema`'s fixed prefix at `integration.go:64-69`), and
456	`appendKeyComponent` already encodes `int64` key components. So the bucket does not need a new
457	key encoder, a derived column, or a change to `computeKey`:
458	
459	> **Floor the timestamp column in place, then group by it like any other column.**
460	
461	A `BatchTimeBucket` map operator sits immediately before the aggregation and rewrites the
462	timestamp column to its bucket start:
463	
464	```go
465	// bucketStart mirrors pkg/flow/streaming/sliding_window.go:302 getWindowStart,
466	// the formula the TopN pre-aggregation path already uses to assign tumbling
467	// windows. It is exactly DATE_BIN with a Unix-epoch origin.
468	func bucketStart(ts, width int64) int64 { return ts - ts%width }
469	```
470	
471	#### The bucket group must NOT be a hash map over all buckets
472	
473	The obvious implementation — add the bucket to `keyIndices` and let `BatchAggregation`'s
474	`map[string]*aggGroup` hold every `(bucket, tags…)` combination until the scan ends — is the
475	wrong shape for a time-series database. It holds `buckets × tagGroups` live groups, blocks until
476	the last row is read, and then needs a sort to put the series back in time order. All three costs
477	are avoidable, because **the input is already sorted by time**.
478	
479	`applyMeasureQueryOrdering` (`banyand/measure/query.go:286`) sets the default explicitly:
480	
481	```go
482	func applyMeasureQueryOrdering(mqo model.MeasureQueryOptions, result *queryResult) {
483		if mqo.Order == nil {
484			result.ascTS = true
485			result.orderByTS = true      // ← globally timestamp-ascending
486			return
487		}
488		…
489		result.orderByTS = mqo.Order.Type == index.OrderByTypeTime
490	}
491	```
492	
493	and `queryResult.Less` (`:913`) then makes the merge heap compare **timestamp first**, falling
494	back to seriesID only to break ties. An aggregation request carries no `order_by` — the
495	distributed analyzer explicitly skips OrderBy resolution when `Agg != nil`
496	(`distributed.go:248`) — so `Order == nil`, and rows arrive in globally ascending timestamp
497	order with no change to the scan at all. (The non-default branch, `orderByTS == false`, sorts by
498	`sidToIndex` first and is series-major; that is the case the guard below exists for.)
499	
500	Sorted input means a bucket, once left behind, can never receive another row. So:
501	
502	> **Stream the buckets.** Keep groups for the *current* bucket only; when a row's bucket advances,
503	> flush that bucket's groups downstream and reset the map.
504	
505	```
506	rows (time-ascending) ──▶ [bucket B0 groups] flush ──▶ [B1 groups] flush ──▶ [B2 …]
507	                           ^ map holds ONE bucket at a time
508	```
509	
510	Three properties fall out, and they are the reason to prefer this over the map:
511	
512	| | Hash map over all buckets | Streaming |
513	|---|---|---|
514	| Live groups | `buckets × tagGroups` | `tagGroups` (one bucket) |
515	| Emission | blocking — nothing until the scan ends | node-local pipelining — bucket *n* leaves the operator while *n+1* fills |
516	| Output order | needs a sort pass | already bucket-ascending |
517	
518	The 1440× memory multiplier a 24-hour/1-minute query would otherwise carry simply does not exist,
519	and `BatchAggregation`'s `BreakerOperator` contract (`vectorized/operator.go:63` — "buffers all
520	input via Consume, then produces output via NextBatch") relaxes to a pipelined operator for the
521	bucketed case. This also mirrors how the codebase already aggregates over time on the write path:
522	`pkg/flow/streaming` assigns tumbling windows and emits them as they close, using the same
523	`getWindowStart` formula.
524	
525	**"Relaxes to a pipelined operator" is not a small tweak to `BreakerOperator` — it needed a new
526	operator shape.** `BreakerOperator` is driven by `breakerStage`, which fully drains upstream via
527	repeated `Consume` calls before it ever calls the breaker's own `NextBatch` — by contract, not by
528	a fixable oversight. Wrapping `BatchTimeBucket` as a `BreakerOperator` would therefore have pulled
529	every upstream batch, closing every bucket the whole scan will ever produce, before emitting the
530	first one: exactly the `buckets × tagGroups` cost this section exists to avoid, just moved from
531	the group map into an output queue. (This is precisely the failure mode §11's testing strategy
532	calls out under "Pipelining": *"A `BreakerOperator`-shaped implementation passes every correctness
533	test and fails this one."*)
534	
535	The actual fix: `BatchTimeBucket` is a genuine `vectorized.PullOperator` that owns and pulls from
536	its upstream directly inside its own `NextBatch`, rather than being driven by `breakerStage`. It
537	is spliced into the pipeline via a new `PipelineBuilder.Transform(fn func(upstream PullOperator)
538	PullOperator)` method (`pkg/query/vectorized/pipeline.go`) — it closes whatever has been built so
539	far into one concrete `PullOperator`, hands it to `fn`, and makes `fn`'s result the new base for
540	whatever follows. `Transform` is now general pipeline infrastructure, available to any future
541	operator with the same requirement: pull upstream lazily, batch by batch, rather than draining it
542	before serving anything. (COUNT_DISTINCT, §7.3–§7.4, does not need it — it reuses
543	`BatchAggregation`'s existing `Consume`/`NextBatch` contract unchanged.)
544	
545	A related pitfall surfaced during review even after the `PullOperator` rewrite: `BatchTimeBucket`
546	originally still drained a closed bucket's aggregator in one synchronous loop before returning
547	anything. That is harmless for the streaming path (one bucket's groups are bounded by construction
548	either way), but index mode's non-streaming aggregator can represent the *entire* scan — so
549	draining it in one shot re-introduced the same "materialize everything before returning the first
550	batch" shape this whole design exists to avoid, just at the output-queue layer instead of the
551	group-map layer. The fix (`drainMapModeAggregator`) pulls that terminal aggregator one page at a
552	time, interleaved with normal output commits, the same discipline the upstream pull loop already
553	follows. Any future operator that holds one aggregator across an entire unordered scan — a
554	candidate shape for other index-mode fallbacks — should drain it the same way.
555	
556	**Index mode does not get this guarantee, and must not stream.** `query.go:140-147` returns
557	through the index-mode branch *before* the ordering setup above ever runs; `buildIndexQueryResult`
558	passes `mqo.Order` through unchanged (`query.go:506-560`), and with a nil order
559	`storage/index.go:350-374` takes the unsorted filter path and returns the underlying index search
560	order. Timestamps being present in `SeriesData` is not an ordering guarantee. A legal index-mode
561	input can therefore arrive in buckets B, A, B — which would reopen a flushed bucket, or trip the
562	monotonicity guard on a query that is perfectly valid.
563	
564	> **Index-mode bucketed aggregation uses the non-streaming map** — groups keyed on
565	> `(bucket, tags…)` held until the scan ends — rather than the streaming operator. Index mode
566	> stays fully in scope (§2); it simply takes the safe path. Streaming is a part-path optimisation,
567	> and the plan must choose between them on `measureSchema.GetIndexMode()`, not on a runtime guess.
568	
569	The alternative — forcing a verified timestamp sort ahead of the operator for index mode — buys
570	back streaming at the cost of a blocking sort, which is what streaming existed to avoid. The map
571	is the honest trade.
572	
573	**The guard is not optional.** Streaming is correct *only* while the input is time-ordered. If
574	`orderByTS` were ever false on the part path, a bucket would be reopened after being flushed and
575	the query would emit duplicate rows for the same bucket — a silently wrong series, the exact
576	failure class this design exists to remove. Two defences, both required:
577	
578	1. **Analyzer** — reject (or refuse to stream) a bucketed request whose `order_by` resolves to
579	   anything other than time ordering, since that flips `orderByTS` to false.
580	2. **Operator** — assert monotonicity. A row whose bucket is *less* than the current bucket is an
581	   invariant violation; fail loudly rather than emit a second row for a closed bucket. This is one
582	   comparison per row and it converts a silent corruption into a loud error.
583	
584	Everything else downstream is unchanged: `keyIndices` gains the timestamp column index,
585	`computeKey` encodes it, `newGroup` copies it with the existing `copyOneValue`, and every row in
586	a group shares the bucket by construction.
587	
588	Three further consequences to handle:
589	
590	- **Reverse D2 conditionally.** `buildAggOutputLayout` (`aggregation.go:659`) must re-emit the
591	  `RoleTimestamp` column when — and only when — a bucket key is present. Today it never does, and
592	  `plan/build_test.go:221` asserts that; the assertion stays correct for the unbucketed case and
593	  gains a bucketed sibling. The serializer then populates `DataPoint.timestamp` from it, which is
594	  why §5.2 needs no new column name.
595	- **Negative timestamps.** Go's `%` truncates toward zero, so `bucketStart` skews by one bucket
596	  for `ts < 0`. Measure timestamps are Unix milliseconds and the write path rejects
597	  non-positive ones, so this is unreachable — but the helper should floor correctly anyway
598	  rather than depend on a caller's invariant.
599	- **Bucket ≠ segment.** The bucket width is unrelated to `ResourceOpts.segment_interval`, which
600	  is an `IntervalRule` restricted to HOUR/DAY and governs physical segmentation, not query
601	  grouping. A bucket may span segments and a segment may contain many buckets; nothing in the
602	  scan needs to know.
603	
604	**Distributed.** The bucket is a pure function of a value already on the row, so each data node
605	floors independently and no coordination is needed. Node partials become per
606	`(bucket, tag group)`; the liaison reduce must key on the bucket too. Two seams:
607	`distributedGroupByTagNames` (`distributed.go:1131`) returns tag names only and needs to carry
608	the bucket flag, and `resolveKeyIndices` (`reduce.go:169`) resolves `RoleTag` columns only and
609	needs to resolve the `RoleTimestamp` column as the leading key.
610	
611	The streaming property survives the fan-out, because **every node emits buckets in ascending
612	order**, so the liaison holds N sorted streams rather than N unordered heaps. That makes the
613	reduce a k-way merge on the bucket key: a bucket closes as soon as every node has moved past it,
614	and the liaison's live state is one bucket's groups rather than the whole window's. The same
615	`buckets × tagGroups` blow-up is avoided on both sides.
616	
617	Node-side streaming is mandatory (it is where the scan-sized state lives). Liaison-side merging
618	is a refinement worth separating, and the distinction matters for what the design is allowed to
619	claim: the vec distributed path broadcasts and **collects every response before `executeAgg`**
620	(`distributed.go:471-476`, `:638`), so the encoded payload is already fully resident. Merging
621	saves the decoded group state, not the buffering.
622	
623	That is why §2's requirement is worded as *node-local* streaming. Calling the whole query
624	pipelined while the liaison buffers all frames would be false. Genuine end-to-end pipelining
625	would need ordered partial streams, a liaison k-way merge, and cancellation/backpressure plumbing
626	— a separate piece of work, not a property this design delivers. A correct first cut
627	hash-aggregates on `(bucket, tags…)` at the liaison, bounded by what the nodes chose to send.
628	
629	### 7.3 COUNT_DISTINCT on a single node
630	
631	A new `AggCountDistinct` function and a new `aggSlot` variant holding a set of encoded values,
632	keyed by `appendKeyComponent` — the same encoder the group key already uses, which covers every
633	target type the matrix admits.
634	
635	The set itself belongs in `pkg/query/aggregation` (a new `distinct.go`), keeping aggregation
636	semantics in the package that owns them; `aggregation_test.go
637	TestBatchAggregation_DelegatesToAggregationPackage` pins that convention.
638	
639	```go
640	// Distinct accumulates the distinct values of one group.
641	type Distinct interface {
642	    In(key []byte) (added bool) // added is true on first sight; it drives the memory charge
643	    Val() int64
644	    Reset()
645	}
646	```
647	
648	`NewMap`/`NewReduce` (`aggregation.go:62`, `:82`) should keep returning `errUnknownFunc` for
649	`COUNT_DISTINCT`. That is not an oversight but the mechanism by which a `COUNT_DISTINCT` TopN
650	rule is rejected: `banyand/measure/topn_post_processor.go:285` calls `NewMap` and propagates the
651	error rather than mis-aggregating.
652	### 7.4 COUNT_DISTINCT across data nodes
653	
654	Every other function pushes down cleanly: the node reduces to a scalar `Partial` and the liaison
655	combines. `COUNT_DISTINCT` appears to break that, because per-node counts cannot in general be
656	summed — the same value seen on two nodes would count twice.
657	
658	**But it can be pushed down whenever shard placement partitions the value space, and that is
659	decidable statically.** So `COUNT_DISTINCT` pushes down like everything else, and a request that
660	cannot be pushed down is **rejected at analyze time** rather than served by a second, costlier
661	mechanism.
662	
663	**The rejection is uniform across deployment shapes.** A standalone server has no sharding, so it
664	could serve every `COUNT_DISTINCT` correctly — and deliberately does not. The condition is
665	evaluated in the analyzer, which runs identically in both modes, so a query either works
666	everywhere or nowhere. The alternative would let a query pass in a single-node development
667	environment and fail on a cluster, which is a worse failure than never having supported it: the
668	rule *the target must be the entity* is only teachable if it holds unconditionally.
669	
670	#### The decomposability condition
671	
672	Shard placement is deterministic and value-derived, but the values it derives from are **the
673	effective routing key**, which is not always the entity. `Locate` computes an entity-based shard
674	and then *overrides* it with the sharding-key router when one is configured
675	(`pkg/partition/route.go:51-65`); the liaison installs both routes
676	(`discovery.go:93-111`, sharding-key locator at `:428-452`), and the write path picks between
677	them at `liaison/grpc/measure.go:176-181`.
678	
679	> **routingTags** = the measure's `sharding_key` when configured, otherwise its entity tags.
680	
681	This is a supported schema shape, not a rejected input: `CheckShardingKeySubset`
682	(`api/validate/validate.go:228-255`) returns nil for a single entity tag, and a subset failure is
683	logged as a *warning* during create/update (`metadata/schema/property/client.go:779-809`). The
684	repo's own fixtures carry one — `service_instance_float_metric.json` has entity
685	`[service_id, entity_id]` with sharding key `[service_id]`.
686	
687	Every row sharing a set of routing tag values lands on exactly one shard. If fixing the group key
688	and the distinct value pins *every* routing tag, that `(group, value)` pair can exist on only one
689	shard, the per-shard distinct sets for a group are **disjoint**, and disjoint cardinalities add:
690	
691	> **routingTags ⊆ groupByTags ∪ {target}** ⟹ per-shard counts are summable.
692	
693	**This is a sufficient condition, not a necessary one.** Fixed predicates in the query, or a
694	proven functional dependency between tags, can equally pin a routing tag that is not grouped. The
695	design does not model either, so some decomposable queries are rejected. That is a deliberate
696	product gate — see *Policy, not necessity* below — and it should not be described as a
697	mathematical boundary.
698	
699	**Why stating this over entity tags is wrong**, concretely: entity `{e}`, sharding key `{s}`, and
700	`COUNT_DISTINCT(e)` with no grouping on `s`. An entity-based rule accepts it because the target
701	*is* the entity. But the same `e` occurring under two `s` values routes to two shards, each
702	reporting a local count of 1, summing to 2 for one distinct entity.
703	
704	When the condition holds, each node computes its own exact distinct count per `(bucket, group)`
705	and emits **one int64** in the existing `Partial{Value}` shape; the liaison reduces with **SUM**.
706	No new wire type, no new partial shape, and the whole `AggModeMap` → `AggModeReduce` machinery is
707	reused verbatim: `COUNT_DISTINCT` is *"local distinct, global sum"*.
708	
709	#### Multi-stage requests are rejected
710	
711	`(stage, shard, group)` identity decides whether two partials are *replicas*. It does **not**
712	make stage-local distinct counts additive, and an earlier draft wrongly assumed it did.
713	
714	Shards partition the *value* space; stages partition *time* — and a distinct value crosses time.
715	Hot holds group `g` with target set `{e1}`, warm holds `g` with `{e1}`: the true whole-range
716	answer is 1, and summing stage-local cardinalities gives 2. No migration overlap or duplicate
717	timestamp is needed; the same target legitimately occurs at different times in different stages.
718	
719	**Bucketing does not rescue it, and the reason is worth recording.** It is tempting to argue that
720	because stages do not overlap in time, a bucket falls inside one stage. But that non-overlap is
721	not visible to the analyzer: `parseNodeSelector` (`dquery.go:161-189`) only builds *selectors* —
722	it produces no stage time windows — and segment selection is by overlapping physical segment
723	range and retention (`storage/segment.go:612-649`, `tsdb.go:277-299`), not by a query-time
724	lifecycle boundary. Bucket width alone is not proof of single-stage ownership.
725	
726	> **Therefore: reject every resolved multi-stage `COUNT_DISTINCT`, bucketed or not.** Resolve the
727	> requested stages — including the `DefaultStages` fallback, which may list several — and reject
728	> if more than one survives. Never silently drop a stage.
729	
730	Lifting this later requires all of: a per-output-bucket read-ownership invariant that is
731	*enforced and analyzer-visible*, stable effective routing, correct per-shard partials, and
732	replica dedup. Short of that, the alternative is a value-bearing union across stages with its own
733	memory budget — the fallback this design rejects on cost grounds elsewhere.
734	
735	A related caveat with the same shape: `ResourceOpts.ShardNum` can be changed by `UpdateGroup`
736	(`metadata/schema/property/client.go:976-989`). A pure node rebalance that preserves logical
737	shard ids is harmless, but a modulus change creates historical routing domains, and a single
738	*current* shard count does not prove which modulus the older selected parts were written under.
739	Treat unchanged `shard_num` over the queried range as an assumption to establish, not a given.
740	
741	#### The rule, and what it means in practice
742	
743	For the common SkyWalking shape the condition collapses to something easy to predict. Those
744	measures declare both entity and sharding key as the single `entity_id` tag — visible in this
745	repo's fixtures, e.g. `pkg/test/measure/testdata/measures/endpoint_resp_time_minute.json`:
746	
747	```json
748	"entity":       { "tag_names": ["entity_id"] },
749	"sharding_key": { "tag_names": ["entity_id"] },
750	"interval": "1m"
751	```
752	
753	With `routingTags = {entity_id}`, `COUNT_DISTINCT(entity_id)` satisfies
754	`routingTags ⊆ groupBy ∪ {target}` for any grouping, and a distinct over a non-routing tag such
755	as `service_id` does not.
756	
757	**The shorthand "distinct over the entity is always supported" is wrong** and was removed: it
758	holds only when the routing key *is* the entity. A measure with a narrower sharding key —
759	entity `[service_id, entity_id]`, sharding key `[service_id]`, as in
760	`service_instance_float_metric.json` — behaves differently in both directions. There,
761	`COUNT_DISTINCT(entity_id)` grouped by `service_id` is accepted because `{service_id}` is
762	covered, while an ungrouped `COUNT_DISTINCT(entity_id)` is rejected. **Always evaluate the
763	condition against `routingTags`, never against a remembered rule about entities.**
764	
765	Applied to the motivating workload, whose measures route on `entity_id`:
766	
767	| Case | Shape | Outcome |
768	|---|---|---|
769	| Distinct api-keys for one user | `COUNT_DISTINCT(entity_id) WHERE service_id = …` | ✅ pushed down |
770	| Distinct api-keys per user | `GROUP BY service_id, COUNT_DISTINCT(entity_id)` | ✅ pushed down |
771	| The same, per time bucket, single stage | `+ TIME_BUCKET(w)` | ✅ pushed down |
772	| Any of the above resolving to **more than one stage** | — | ❌ rejected |
773	| Distinct *models* per user, as modelled today | model is inside a serialized blob, not a tag | ❌ not expressible at any layer |
774	| Distinct models, with the model promoted to an entity | structurally identical to the api-key case | ✅ pushed down |
775	| "How many distinct users exist?" | `COUNT_DISTINCT(service_id)` — not a routing tag | ❌ rejected |
776	
777	Every case this workload expresses is pushed down, **provided it resolves to a single stage** —
778	which is now a live constraint on the deployment, not a footnote, since an empty `stages` falls
779	back to `DefaultStages` and that may list several.
780	
781	#### Why rejection rather than a fallback
782	
783	A fallback path — nodes shipping their distinct *values* for the liaison to union — is always
784	correct and needs no condition check. It was considered and rejected (§9), because:
785	
786	- **Its cost is unbounded and user-controlled.** Wire volume and liaison memory scale with
787	  cardinality, so one `COUNT_DISTINCT` over a high-cardinality tag funnels every value into a
788	  single process. "Slow and correct" is a poor trade when the liaison is shared infrastructure;
789	  the failure lands on every other query in flight.
790	- **It makes the cost model unpredictable.** Two queries that look alike would differ by orders
791	  of magnitude depending on a schema property the author cannot see in the query text. A hard
792	  rule — *the target must be the entity* — is something a user can reason about in advance.
793	- **It doubles the surface.** Two implementations of one function, a static chooser between them,
794	  opposite replica-dedup requirements (union is idempotent, summation is not), and a differential
795	  test to keep them honest — all to serve queries the data model says should be written
796	  differently.
797	- **It is inconsistent with the rest of this design**, which already rejects rather than
798	  approximates: array and timestamp tags (§6), numeric functions over string tags (§6), bucket
799	  a bucket width with no source to resolve it from (§5.3), tag aggregation on the row engine (§8).
800	
801	Rejection is also the honest signal. A `COUNT_DISTINCT` over a non-entity tag is usually a
802	modelling mismatch, and the error should say so rather than silently serving it expensively:
803	
804	```
805	count_distinct(service_id) is not supported: the target must be part of the measure's
806	entity (entity_id), or every entity tag must appear in GROUP BY. Either group by
807	service_id and count_distinct(entity_id), or model service_id as an entity tag.
808	```
809	
810	The user is not stuck: `GROUP BY <target>` and counting the returned rows client-side still
811	works exactly as it does today, and is the same shape the fallback would have implemented — only
812	with the cost visible to the caller who chose it.
813	
814	#### Policy, not necessity
815	
816	Three of the rejections above are **product decisions and should be read as such**, not as
817	mathematical boundaries:
818	
819	- The condition is *sufficient*, not necessary. Fixed predicates and proven functional
820	  dependencies could pin an ungrouped routing tag; this design models neither.
821	- Grouping by every effective routing tag can make a **non-routing target** decomposable. Such
822	  queries are rejected because the analyzer does not reason about it, not because they are
823	  unanswerable.
824	- Rejecting uniformly in standalone (§7.4) forgoes queries a single node could union locally and
825	  exactly. That is a portability choice — one contract regardless of deployment shape — and is
826	  only defensible while it is stated deliberately rather than presented as a limit of the maths.
827	
828	Each is a place where the engine could later do more without changing any wire format. Recording
829	them as policy keeps that door visible; describing them as necessity would quietly close it.
830	
831	#### De-duplicating the partials
832	
833	Replicas of a shard hold identical data, so selecting one copy per replica set is the right
834	mechanism. It needs two fixes to be correct, because today's deduped unit is neither a shard nor
835	a stage.
836	
837	**(a) Today's partial is per-node, and its shard label is a hint.** `computeKey`
838	(`aggregation.go:523`) builds the group key from `keyIndices` — the group-by tags only — and
839	`newGroup` stamps the group with the shard id of the *first row that created it*. A node holding
840	shards 1 and 2 emits **one** partial for group `g` covering both, labelled with whichever shard
841	appeared first. "The replicas are all the same" is true of shards and not of these partials.
842	
843	Within a node each shard appears exactly once — there are no duplicate shards on a node — so a
844	per-shard partial is always well defined. That property is what makes the fix below *correct*;
845	it is not what makes today's labelling *sufficient*. What breaks today is that node shard-*sets*
846	differ, and under replication they do, by construction:
847	
848	```go
849	// pkg/node/round_robin.go:218
850	func (r *roundRobinSelector) selectNode(index int, replicasID uint32) string {
851		adjustedIndex := index + int(replicasID)
852		return r.nodes[adjustedIndex%len(r.nodes)]
853	}

859	|---|---|---|---|---|
860	| replica 0 | n0 | n1 | n2 | n3 |
861	| replica 1 | n1 | n2 | n3 | n0 |
862

127	// which preserves any tag the request projected even when it is not a
128	// GroupBy key.
129	//
130	// Output rows are emitted one per group, in group-insertion order,
131	// paginated by batchSize.

133		dedupSeen        map[string]struct{}
134		outputSchema     *vectorized.BatchSchema
135		pool             *vectorized.BatchPool
136		tracker          *vectorized.MemoryTracker
137		span             *query.Span
138		groups           map[string]*aggGroup
139		inputSchema      *vectorized.BatchSchema
140		aggValuePath     AggValuePath
141		tagIndices       []int
142		aggs             []AggSpec
143		aggOutOffsets    []int
144		aggHasCount      []bool
145		keyIndices       []int
146		aggInputCountIdx []int
147		insertion        []*aggGroup
148		outputShardIdx   int
149		outputTimeIdx    int
150		tagOutOffset     int
151		mode             AggMode
152		shardIDIdx       int
153		bucketIdx        int
154		entrySize        int64

156		rowsIn           int64
157		rowsOut          int64

163	// aggGroup carries one group's reduction state plus a copy of every
164	// projected tag column for this group. tagCols is indexed by position in
165	// BatchAggregation.tagIndices (NOT just the GroupBy keys), so non-key
166	// projected tags can be emitted as their first-seen value.
167	//
168	// shardID is captured by newGroup from the input batch's RoleShardID column
169	// at the first row that created the group, matching the row path's
170	// incidental "first-idp-of-group" rule (G9f.2.a; see
171	// pkg/query/logical/measure/measure_plan_aggregation.go:285). It is only
172	// read by AggModeMap emit; AggModeAll ignores it. Stays zero when
173	// keyIndices is empty (scalar reduce) so the emitted partial matches the
174	// row path's aggAllIterator.Current() hardcoding ShardId: 0.
175	//
176	// timeValue is captured by newGroup from the input batch's (already
177	// bucket-floored) RoleTimestamp column at the group's creating row, exactly
178	// like shardID — it is constant for every row in the group by construction,
179	// since the bucket-floored timestamp is itself part of the group key
180	// (design §7.2). Read only when bucketIdx >= 0; ignored otherwise.
181	type aggGroup struct {
182		key       string
183		tagCols   []vectorized.Column
184		slots     []aggSlot
185		shardID   int64
186		timeValue int64
187	}

189	// aggSlot holds either:
190	//
191	//   - AggModeAll / AggModeMap: an aggregation.Map of int64 or float64
192	//     (Consume folds raw values; emit reads Val() / Partial()).
193	//   - AggModeReduce:           an aggregation.Reduce of int64 or float64
194	//     (Consume reads Partial state from the input columns and Combine()s;
195	//     emit reads Val() to produce the final reduced value).
196	//
197	// Whether int or float is decided at construction time by AggFunc + input
198	// column type:
199	//
200	//   - SUM/MIN/MAX: matches input type (preserve precision).
201	//   - COUNT:        always int64.
202	//   - MEAN:         always float64 (so int inputs yield fractional means).
203	//
204	// Exactly one of intMap/floatMap is non-nil in Map/All mode; exactly one of
205	// intReduce/floatReduce is non-nil in Reduce mode.
206	type aggSlot struct {
207		intMap      aggregation.Map[int64]
208		floatMap    aggregation.Map[float64]
209		intReduce   aggregation.Reduce[int64]
210		floatReduce aggregation.Reduce[float64]
211		// distinct backs AggCountDistinct only (AggModeAll/AggModeMap). It is
212		// not Number-parameterized like intMap/floatMap, since the target may
213		// be a string/bytes tag, not just numeric — see foldDistinct.
214		distinct     aggregation.Distinct
215		fn           AggFunc
216		inputIsFloat bool
217	}

219	// NewBatchAggregation constructs a BatchAggregation. It builds the output
220	// schema internally (keys + agg outputs) and owns its output BatchPool.
221	//
222	// tracker carries the per-pipeline memory budget; entrySize is the bytes
223	// reserved per new group bucket (key columns + slots + map entry overhead).
224	// Pass entrySize=0 to disable per-group bookkeeping. tracker must not be nil
225	// — use a large NewMemoryTracker for unit tests that don't care about budget.
226	//
227	// Time bucketing (design §7.2) needs no dedicated parameter: when keyIndices
228	// contains a RoleTimestamp column, that column is treated as the bucket key
229	// — grouping by it is already handled generically by computeKey, and the
230	// only bucket-specific behavior (conditional D2 reversal: re-emitting the
231	// bucket start as a RoleTimestamp output column) is derived here from that
232	// same column. RoleTimestamp never legitimately appears in keyIndices for
233	// any other reason, so this inference is unambiguous.
234	func NewBatchAggregation(
235		input *vectorized.BatchSchema, keyIndices []int,
236		aggs []AggSpec, mode AggMode, batchSize int,
237		tracker *vectorized.MemoryTracker, entrySize int64,
238	) *BatchAggregation {
239		bucketIdx := -1
240		for _, idx := range keyIndices {
241			if input.Columns[idx].Role == vectorized.RoleTimestamp {
242				bucketIdx = idx
243				break
244			}
245		}
246		tagIndices := collectTagIndices(input, keyIndices, hiddenTagExclusionSet(aggs))
247		layout := buildAggOutputLayout(input, tagIndices, aggs, mode, bucketIdx)
248		return &BatchAggregation{
249			inputSchema:      input,
250			outputSchema:     layout.schema,
251			pool:             vectorized.NewBatchPool(layout.schema, batchSize),
252			tracker:          tracker,
253			keyIndices:       slices.Clone(keyIndices),
254			tagIndices:       tagIndices,
255			aggs:             slices.Clone(aggs),
256			aggOutOffsets:    layout.aggOutOffsets,
257			aggHasCount:      layout.aggHasCount,
258			outputShardIdx:   layout.outputShardIdx,
259			outputTimeIdx:    layout.outputTimestampIdx,
260			tagOutOffset:     layout.tagOutOffset,
261			shardIDIdx:       findShardIDIndex(input),
262			bucketIdx:        bucketIdx,
263			aggInputCountIdx: buildAggInputCountIdx(input, aggs, mode),
264			mode:             mode,
265			aggValuePath:     deriveAggValuePath(input, aggs),
266			batchSize:        batchSize,
267			entrySize:        entrySize,
268		}
269	}

271	// deriveAggValuePath inspects the pre-built AggSpec list to determine which
272	// column-type path was used. If any spec's InputCol points to a
273	// ColumnTypeFieldValue column the path is AggValuePathFieldValueFallback;
274	// otherwise it is AggValuePathTyped. AggValuePathUnresolved is never returned
275	// here — callers that build AggSpecs have already verified the columns exist.
276	func deriveAggValuePath(input *vectorized.BatchSchema, aggs []AggSpec) AggValuePath {
277		for _, spec := range aggs {
278			if spec.InputCol >= 0 && spec.InputCol < len(input.Columns) {
279				if input.Columns[spec.InputCol].Type == vectorized.ColumnTypeFieldValue {
280					return AggValuePathFieldValueFallback
281				}
282			}
283		}
284		return AggValuePathTyped
285	}
